title: EU imposes 9.5% anti-dumping duty on Indian cold-rolled steel
intro: The European Union's definitive anti-dumping duty on cold-rolled steel leads today's edition. Business Standard and KNN India report a 9.5% duty on Indian cold-rolled steel, and EU Law Live notes that the measure also covers imports from Japan, Taiwan, Türkiye and Vietnam. The material does not give the duty's duration, the products covered in detail or company-specific rates. Tata Steel dominates the corporate news. Mint reports that its 40 mtpa domestic capacity target has slipped by three to five years, while The Hindu BusinessLine reports that the company is now eyeing 50 mt in India. JSW Steel and JFE Steel have unveiled a joint venture, and the government is drafting a National Steel Policy 2047. There are no price reports in today's material.

marketOverview: Today's material contains no steel price data, and the Steel Price Developments section has no articles. Readers should not infer price direction from this edition. The conditions described are structural rather than transactional. According to The Tribune, T V Narendran said Chinese steel exports could reach 130 million tonnes in 2026. Business Standard reports that India's top steelmakers have flagged high production costs alongside the threat from Chinese imports. On demand, News On AIR quotes the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel as saying that domestic consumption has doubled to 152 MT in a decade. KNN India reports that capacity has crossed 220 million tonnes. None of the excerpts gives price levels, spreads or inventory data.

analysis: Analysis: The day's reports set two pressures against each other. Externally, the EU's 9.5% duty on Indian cold-rolled steel narrows one export outlet. Narendran's warning, reported by The Tribune, that Chinese exports could reach 130 million tonnes in 2026 points to continued competition for every open market, including India's own. This could increase pressure on New Delhi to strengthen trade defences, a direction the Indian Steel Association's statement on unfairly priced imports appears to support. Domestically, the ambition remains large. The draft policy figure of 600 million tonnes, Tata Steel's 50 mt goal and the JSW JFE venture all suggest that producers are betting on home demand, which News On AIR reports has doubled to 152 MT. The slippage in Tata Steel's 40 mtpa target, however, is a reminder that execution, land and raw-material access may constrain growth more than demand does. This is why producers' requests on land and iron ore reform in the 2047 policy could matter. Readers should treat the capacity figures as targets; the material provides no funding or timeline detail.
